diagram_name: Match the Activity to the Skill
learning_objective: The learner will classify ten afternoon activities by the human skill each builds most directly, correctly placing at least eight of ten on the first attempt.
specification:
Type: microsim **sim-id:** match-activity-to-skill
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified
**Bloom Level:** Understand
**Bloom Verb:** classify
**Learning Objective:** The learner will classify ten afternoon activities by the human skill each builds most directly, correctly placing at least eight of ten on the first attempt. **Prerequisites:** collaboration, communication skills, empathy, creativity, computational thinking, and the activity-skill matrix (all defined in Chapters 12 and 13 and in the section "Matching Activities to Skills" above). **Evidence of Mastery:** The learner places each of 10 activities in one of five skill bins and submits it. A placement is correct when it matches the "Primary skill" column in Content. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt. Reading the matrix is exploration, not evidence. **Misconceptions:** (1) Each activity builds only one skill. (2) Technical activities do not need collaboration. (3) Arts activities build only creativity. **Instructional Rationale:** Choosing the primary skill requires reading what the activity asks students to do most directly. Feedback names the other skills the activity builds, so the learner sees that the single answer is a primary emphasis and not an exclusive one. **Content:** Five bins with definitions shown on request: | Skill | Definition shown | |---|---| | Collaboration | Working with others so that each contribution shapes the result | | Communication | Expressing ideas to others and understanding theirs | | Empathy | Understanding and sharing another person's feelings and view | | Creativity | Producing ideas or products that are new and valuable | | Computational thinking | Breaking problems into parts, finding patterns, abstracting, and writing precise steps | Ten activities: | # | Activity shown to the learner | Primary skill | Why (shown as feedback) | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Rehearsing a piece in an orchestra where every part depends on the others. | Collaboration | Each player's part shapes the whole; it also builds listening and timing. | | 2 | Playing a team sport where players must pass and cover for each other. | Collaboration | Success depends on coordinated roles; it also builds communication. | | 3 | Presenting a project to a panel of community members and answering their questions. | Communication | The main demand is expressing ideas to an audience; it also builds confidence. | | 4 | Debating a motion in front of an audience. | Communication | The main demand is making and defending a case aloud; it also builds perspective taking. | | 5 | Tutoring a younger student in reading each week and reflecting on how they felt. | Empathy | The main demand is understanding another person's experience; it also builds communication. | | 6 | Interviewing residents of a care home about their lives. | Empathy | The main demand is understanding another person's view; it also builds listening. | | 7 | Designing and painting a mural from the student's own idea. | Creativity | The main demand is producing something new; it also builds craft. | | 8 | Improvising scenes in theater games, producing many ideas in a few minutes. | Creativity | The main demand is generating many new ideas; it also builds spontaneity. | | 9 | Programming a robot to follow a line and debugging it when it fails. | Computational thinking | The main demand is decomposing, testing, and writing precise steps; it also builds collaboration. | | 10 | Writing a program that sorts a list of names. | Computational thinking | The main demand is writing a precise procedure; it also builds persistence. | **Provenance:** The matrix follows the chapter section "Matching Activities to Skills." The activities are illustrative, written for this chapter. **Rules:** Each activity has exactly one correct primary skill, given in Content, and each skill has exactly two activities. An activity is scored on its first submitted placement only. The score counts first-attempt correct placements out of 10. Mastery is a score >= 8. **Learner Activity:** 1. The learner sees one activity at a time and the five skills. 2. The learner places the activity and submits it. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the feedback text, including the other skills the activity builds. 3. If incorrect, the learner may place it again; the second attempt does not change the score. After the second attempt, the correct skill and reason are shown. 4. After all 10 activities, the sim shows the score and the misplaced activities with their correct skills. 5. The learner should notice that each skill is the primary skill of two activities, and that every activity also builds a second skill. **Feedback:** 10 activities, shuffled once per session, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: [skill]. [Why text]." Incorrect: "Not quite. Think about what the activity asks students to do most directly. [Why text for the correct answer, without naming the skill]." After the second attempt the correct skill is revealed and the activity counts as missed. A running score "First-try correct: n of 10" is shown. Final message for a score >= 8: "You can match activities to the skills they build." For a score < 8: "Review the five skills and try again; the activities will be reshuffled." **Starting State:** Activity 1 of the shuffled order is shown with the five skills, the score "First-try correct: 0 of 10," and the prompt "Which skill does this activity build most directly?" **Chapter Anchors:** The chapter's matrix lists five primary skills, collaboration, communication, empathy, creativity, and computational thinking, with the same example activities. The mastery bar is 8 of 10.
